name: Mr. Bender and Square
description: Mr. Bender has a digital table of size n × n , each cell can be switched on or off. He wants the field to have at least c switched on squares. When this condition is fulfilled, Mr Bender will be happy. We'll consider the table rows numbered from top to bottom from 1 to n , and the columns — numbered from left to right from 1 to n . Initially there is exactly one switched on cell with coordinates ( x , y ) ( x is the row number, y is the column number), and all other cells are switched off. Then each second we switch on the cells that are off but have the side-adjacent cells that are on. For a cell with coordinates ( x , y ) the side-adjacent cells are cells with coordinates ( x - 1, y ) , ( x + 1, y ) , ( x , y - 1) , ( x , y + 1) . In how many seconds will Mr. Bender get happy?
input_specification: The first line contains four space-separated integers n , x , y , c (1 ≤ n , c ≤ 10 9 ; 1 ≤ x , y ≤ n ; c ≤ n 2 ) .
output_specification: In a single line print a single integer — the answer to the problem.
approach_summary: Verify predicate monotonicity: P(x) is true for x ≤ K and false otherwise. Binary search over the answer domain to find the boundary in O(log(Range) × Verify_Time).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 255D — Mr. Bender and Square [33. Binary Search]
topic_editorial.summary: Binary search on the monotonic answer domain.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The predicate function $P(x)$ ('Is answer $\le x$ feasible?') is monotonic: if $P(x)$ is true for some value, it remains true for all larger values (or vice versa). This allows binary division of the answer search space $[\text{low}, \text{high}]$ in $O(\log(\text{Range}))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N \log(\text{Range}))$
  The binary search divides the search interval by 2 at each iteration, requiring $\log_2(\text{Range})$ steps. In each step, the feasibility check `check(mid)` scans the array in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(1)$ auxiliary space
  The algorithm operates directly over the input array without allocating extra auxiliary memory.
